disclaimer: Heartbeat supports self-assessment only. It is not a medical device and does not diagnose. Ranges are demo values for a healthy adult at rest, drawn from public clinical references; they are not flight-surgeon approved.
intervalRule: Each band covers min <= value < max. A missing min means no lower limit; a missing max means no upper limit. Bands of one indicator never overlap and leave no gaps.

watch.message: Recheck this indicator at your next check-up. Mission control can see this result after the next sync.

critical.message: Tell your crew medical officer now. This result is flagged for the flight surgeons on the ground and will be sent at the next sync.

csa-radiation.title: Radiation and astronaut health (Canadian Space Agency)

indicators.name: Blood pressure
indicators.whyItMatters: In microgravity, body fluids shift toward the head and the heart and blood vessels adapt. This can change blood pressure and cause dizziness or fainting when gravity returns.
howToMeasure: Sit or strap in and rest quietly for 5 minutes first.
Put the cuff on your bare upper arm at heart level.
Do not talk or move during the reading.
Take two readings 1 minute apart and enter the second one.
indicators.risks: Persistently high pressure strains the heart and vessels. Low pressure can cause light-headedness and fainting.

value.label: Very low systolic
guidance: Lie down with your legs restrained and raised if you can.
Drink fluids if you are able to.
Tell your crew medical officer now.

value.label: Low systolic
guidance: Drink water and recheck in 30 minutes.
Move slowly and avoid sudden position changes.

value.label: Normal systolic
guidance: Keep up your exercise countermeasures and hydration.

value.label: High systolic
guidance: Rest for 10 minutes and measure again.
Limit salt in your next meals.
Check that you are doing your scheduled exercise.

value.label: Very high systolic
guidance: Stop any exercise and rest.
Measure again in 5 minutes.
Tell your crew medical officer now, especially with headache, chest pain or vision changes.

secondaryValue.label: Very low diastolic
guidance: Lie down, drink fluids if able, and tell your crew medical officer now.

secondaryValue.label: Low diastolic
guidance: Drink water and recheck in 30 minutes.

secondaryValue.label: Normal diastolic
guidance: No action needed.

secondaryValue.label: High diastolic
guidance: Rest for 10 minutes and measure again.
Limit salt in your next meals.

secondaryValue.label: Very high diastolic
guidance: Stop any exercise, rest, and tell your crew medical officer now.

indicators.name: Heart rate
indicators.whyItMatters: Without gravity the heart works less and can lose conditioning. Changes in resting heart rate can show deconditioning, stress, fever or dehydration.
howToMeasure: Use the pulse sensor, or count your wrist pulse for 30 seconds and multiply by 2.
Do not measure right after exercise.
indicators.risks: A very slow or very fast resting pulse can mean a heart rhythm problem, dehydration or infection.

bands.label: Very slow
guidance: Recheck now while resting.
If you feel dizzy, faint or short of breath, tell your crew medical officer now.

bands.label: Slow
guidance: Fit astronauts can rest below 50; recheck at your next check-up.
Note any dizziness or tiredness.

bands.label: Normal
guidance: Keep up your exercise countermeasures.

bands.label: Fast
guidance: Rest for 10 minutes and measure again.
Drink water; check your temperature for fever.
Avoid caffeine until it settles.

bands.label: Very fast
guidance: Stop all activity and rest.
Tell your crew medical officer now, especially with chest pain or palpitations.

indicators.name: Blood sugar
indicators.whyItMatters: Limited food choices, stress and inactivity in a closed habitat can change how the body handles sugar. Low sugar affects alertness, which matters for safety-critical tasks.
howToMeasure: Prick the side of a fingertip with the lancet and put the drop on the test strip.
Note whether you ate in the last 2 hours; fasting values are most reliable.
indicators.risks: Low sugar can cause shakiness, confusion and fainting. High sugar over time harms vessels and nerves.

bands.label: Very low
guidance: Eat or drink 15 g of fast sugar now (juice, glucose gel).
Recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still low.
Tell your crew medical officer now.

bands.label: Low
guidance: Eat 15 g of fast sugar and recheck in 15 minutes.
Do not skip planned meals.

bands.label: Normal
guidance: Keep regular meal times.

bands.label: High
guidance: Recheck fasting before your next meal.
Choose fewer sugary items from the menu.
Drink water.

bands.label: Very high
guidance: Drink water and recheck now.
Tell your crew medical officer now, especially with thirst, nausea or confusion.

indicators.name: Body temperature
indicators.whyItMatters: The immune system changes in spaceflight, and germs spread easily in a closed habitat. Fever is often the first sign of infection.
howToMeasure: Wait 15 minutes after eating, drinking or exercise.
Place the thermometer under your tongue with your mouth closed until it beeps.
Enter the value with one decimal, in °C.
indicators.risks: Fever suggests infection; a low temperature can mean hypothermia or a bad reading.

bands.label: Very low
guidance: Measure again to rule out a bad reading.
Warm up with extra layers.
Tell your crew medical officer now if it stays low.

bands.label: Low
guidance: Measure again in 30 minutes.
Add a layer of clothing.

bands.label: Normal
guidance: No action needed.

bands.label: Fever
guidance: Rest and drink fluids.
Wash hands and limit close contact with crewmates.
Measure again in 4 hours.

bands.label: High fever
guidance: Rest, drink fluids and isolate where possible.
Tell your crew medical officer now.

indicators.name: Sleep
indicators.whyItMatters: Noise, light, shifted schedules and 16 sunrises a day in orbit disrupt sleep. Too little sleep hurts mood, attention and the ability to do safe work.
howToMeasure: Enter the total hours you slept in the last 24 hours, including naps.
Use the sleep log or wearable if you have one; otherwise estimate.
indicators.risks: Ongoing short sleep raises the chance of errors, low mood and weaker immunity.

bands.label: Severely short
guidance: Avoid safety-critical tasks until you have rested if the schedule allows.
Tell your crew medical officer so the schedule can be adjusted.

bands.label: Short
guidance: Plan a nap if the schedule allows.
Dim lights and screens an hour before your sleep period.
Avoid caffeine in the 6 hours before sleep.

bands.label: Normal
guidance: Keep a regular sleep period.

bands.label: Long
guidance: Long sleep can be a sign of illness or low mood; check your temperature and mood.

indicators.name: Mood
indicators.whyItMatters: Months of isolation, confinement and distance from family affect behavioral health. Noticing low mood early helps prevent bigger problems.
howToMeasure: Think about how you have felt overall today.
Click the face that fits best. There is no wrong answer.
indicators.risks: Low mood that lasts can affect sleep, teamwork and performance.

bands.label: Very bad
guidance: You do not have to handle this alone; talk to a crewmate or your crew medical officer today.
Ask for a private conference with the flight psychologist.

bands.label: Bad
guidance: Take a short break, exercise, or call family at the next opportunity.
If it lasts more than 2 days, talk to your crew medical officer.

bands.label: Okay to very good
guidance: Keep up the routines that help you.
